questions.question: Gauss-Seidel method is used to solve the following equations (as per the given order): [latex]x_{1}+2x_{2}+3x_{3}=5[/latex] [latex]2x_{1}+3x_{2}+x_{3}=1[/latex] [latex]3x_{1}+2x_{2}+x_{3}=3[/latex] Assuming initial guess as [latex]x_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}=0[/latex] , the value of [latex]x_{3}[/latex] after the first iteration is __________
questions.explanation: The equations are [latex] x_{1}+2 x_{2}+3 x_{3}=5 \quad \ldots(3)[/latex] [latex] 2 x_{1}+3 x_{2}+x_{3}=1 \quad \ldots(2)[/latex] [latex] 3 x_{1}+2 x_{2}+x_{3}=3 \quad \ldots(1)[/latex] By poveting we can write [latex] \begin{aligned} 3 x_{1}+2 x_{2}+x_{3} &=3 \\ 2 x_{1}+3 x_{2}+x_{3} &=1 \\ x_{1} &=\frac{3-2 x_{2}-x_{3}}{3} \quad \ldots(1)\\ x_{2} &=\frac{1-2 x_{1}-x_{3}}{3} \quad \ldots(2)\\ x_{1}+2 x_{2}+3 x_{3} &=5 \\ x_{3} &=\frac{5-x_{1}-2 x_{2}}{3} \quad \ldots(3) \end{aligned}[/latex] Put [latex] x_{2}=0 \quad x_{3}=0 [/latex] in equation (1) [latex] x_{1}=1[/latex] Put [latex]x_{1}=1 \quad x_{3}=0 [/latex] in equation (3) [latex] x_{2}=-0.333 [/latex] Put [latex]x_{1}=1 \quad x_{2}=-0.333 [/latex] in equation [latex] (3) [/latex] [latex] x_{3}=1.555[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
The equations are
[latex] x_{1}+2 x_{2}+3 x_{3}=5 \quad \ldots(3)[/latex]
[latex] 2 x_{1}+3 x_{2}+x_{3}=1 \quad \ldots(2)[/latex]
[latex] 3 x_{1}+2 x_{2}+x_{3}=3 \quad \ldots(1)[/latex]
By poveting we can write
[latex] \begin{aligned} 3 x_{1}+2 x_{2}+x_{3} &=3 \\ 2 x_{1}+3 x_{2}+x_{3} &=1 \\ x_{1} &=\frac{3-2 x_{2}-x_{3}}{3} \quad \ldots(1)\\ x_{2} &=\frac{1-2 x_{1}-x_{3}}{3} \quad \ldots(2)\\ x_{1}+2 x_{2}+3 x_{3} &=5 \\ x_{3} &=\frac{5-x_{1}-2 x_{2}}{3} \quad \ldots(3) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Put [latex] x_{2}=0 \quad x_{3}=0 [/latex] in equation (1)
[latex] x_{1}=1[/latex]
Put [latex]x_{1}=1 \quad x_{3}=0 [/latex] in equation (3)
[latex] x_{2}=-0.333 [/latex]
Put [latex]x_{1}=1 \quad x_{2}=-0.333 [/latex] in equation [latex] (3) [/latex]
[latex] x_{3}=1.555[/latex]

questions.explanation: [latex] \begin{aligned} \int_{c}^{\int \nabla \phi \cdot \sigma F} &=\int_{c}(y z \bar{i}+x z \bar{\rho}+x y \bar{k}) \\ &\qquad \qquad \quad (dx\bar{i}+dx\bar{\rho}+dz\bar{k})\\ &=\int_{c} y z d x+x z d y+x y d z\\ &=\int_{c} d(x y z) \\ &=(x y z) \\ \text { Given that } x &=t, y=t^{2}, z=3 t^{2} \\ &=\left.\left(t \cdot t^{2} \cdot 3 t^{2}\right)\right|_{1} ^{3}\\ &=\left.3\left(t^{5}\right)\right|_{1} ^{3}\\ &=3\left(3^{5}-1\right) \\ &=3^{6}-3=729-3=726 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: A single degree of freedom spring mass system with viscous damping has a spring constant of 10 kN/m. The system is excited by a sinusoidal force of amplitude 100 N. If the damping factor(ratio) is 0.25, the amplitude of steady state oscillation at resonance is ________mm.

Forcing function [latex]=F_{0} \sin \omega t [/latex]
Given, [latex]F_{0}=100 \mathrm{N} [/latex]
Damping factor,
[latex] \xi=0.25[/latex]
Spring constant
[latex] \begin{aligned} k&=10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}=10 \times 1000=10000 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m} \\ A&=\frac{F_{0} / \mathrm{k}}{\sqrt{\left\{1-\left(\frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}\right)^{2}\right\}^{2}+\left(2 \xi \frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}\right)^{2}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
At resonance
[latex] \begin{aligned} \omega &=\omega_{n} \\ \therefore \quad A &=\frac{100}{10000}=\frac{0.01}{2 \xi}=0.02 \mathrm{m} \\ &=20 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Propane (C3H8) is burned in an oxygen atmosphere with 10% deficit oxygen with respect to the stoichiometric requirement. Assuming no hydrocarbons in the products, the volume percentage of CO in the products is __________
questions.explanation: For stoichiometric burning (i.e., chemically correct), number of moles of [latex]\mathrm{O}_{2}[/latex] required =5. As it si burnt with 10 % deficient \mathrm{O}_{2} , it will generate CO. That is, the new equation is [latex] \mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+0.9 \times 5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \alpha \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\beta \mathrm{CO}+\gamma \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}[/latex] Balancing carbon atoms, we get [latex] 3=\alpha+\beta \quad \cdots(i)[/latex] Balancing hydrogen atoms, we get [latex] \begin{aligned} 8&=2 \gamma\\ \text{or }\quad \gamma&=4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Balancing oxygen atoms, we get [latex] \begin{aligned} 0.9 \times 10 &=2 \alpha+\beta+\gamma \\ 9 &=2 \alpha+\beta+4 \\ 5 &=2 \alpha+\beta\quad \cdots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex] Eq. (ii) - Eq. (i), we get [latex] \begin{aligned} 2&=\alpha\\ \text{or }\quad \alpha&=2 \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+\mathrm{aO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{bCO}_{2}+\mathrm{cH}_{2} \mathrm{O}[/latex] Balancing carbon atoms, we get [latex] \begin{aligned} 3&=b\\ \text{or } \quad b&=3\\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Balancing hydrogen atoms, we get [latex] \begin{aligned} 8&=2 c\\ \text{or}\quad c&=4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Balancing oxygen atoms, we get [latex] \begin{aligned} 2 a &=2 b+c \\ 2 a &=2 \times 3+4=10 \\ a &=5 \end{aligned}[/latex] Substituting [latex]\alpha=2[/latex] in Eq. (ii), we get [latex] \begin{array}{l} \quad 5=2 \times 2 \times \beta \\ \text { or } \quad \beta=1 \\ \therefore \mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+4.5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{CO}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \end{array}[/latex] The volume percentage of CO in the product [latex] \begin{array}{l} =\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}\right) \times 100 \\ =\left(\frac{1}{2+1+4}\right) \times 100 \\ =14.28 \% \end{array}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
For stoichiometric burning (i.e., chemically correct),
number of moles of [latex]\mathrm{O}_{2}[/latex] required =5.
As it si burnt with 10 % deficient \mathrm{O}_{2} , it will generate CO.
That is, the new equation is
[latex] \mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+0.9 \times 5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \alpha \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\beta \mathrm{CO}+\gamma \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}[/latex]
Balancing carbon atoms, we get
[latex] 3=\alpha+\beta \quad \cdots(i)[/latex]
Balancing hydrogen atoms, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 8&=2 \gamma\\ \text{or }\quad \gamma&=4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Balancing oxygen atoms, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 0.9 \times 10 &=2 \alpha+\beta+\gamma \\ 9 &=2 \alpha+\beta+4 \\ 5 &=2 \alpha+\beta\quad \cdots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Eq. (ii) - Eq. (i), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2&=\alpha\\ \text{or }\quad \alpha&=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+\mathrm{aO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{bCO}_{2}+\mathrm{cH}_{2} \mathrm{O}[/latex]
Balancing carbon atoms, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 3&=b\\ \text{or } \quad b&=3\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Balancing hydrogen atoms, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 8&=2 c\\ \text{or}\quad c&=4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Balancing oxygen atoms, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2 a &=2 b+c \\ 2 a &=2 \times 3+4=10 \\ a &=5 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting [latex]\alpha=2[/latex] in Eq. (ii), we get
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \quad 5=2 \times 2 \times \beta \\ \text { or } \quad \beta=1 \\ \therefore \mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+4.5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{CO}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \end{array}[/latex]
The volume percentage of CO in the product
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}\right) \times 100 \\ =\left(\frac{1}{2+1+4}\right) \times 100 \\ =14.28 \% \end{array}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider two hydraulic turbines having identical specific speed and effective head at the inlet. If the speed ratio (N1/N2) of the two turbines is 2, then the respective power ratio (P1/P2) is _____________
questions.explanation: Given data: [latex] \begin{aligned} N_{s 1} &=N_{s 2} \\ H_{1} &=H_{2} \\ \frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}} &=2 \end{aligned}\\ \text{We know that specific speed of the turbine,}\\ \begin{aligned} N_{s}&=\frac{N \sqrt{P}}{H^{5 / 4}}\\ \left(N_{s}\right)_{1} &=\left(N_{s}\right)_{2} \\ \frac{N_{1} \sqrt{P_{1}}}{H_{1}^{5 / 4}} &=\frac{N_{2} \sqrt{P_{2}}}{H_{2}^{5 / 4}} \\ N_{1} \sqrt{P_{1}} &=N_{2} \sqrt{P_{2}} \qquad\therefore H_{1}= h_{2} \\ \text{or}\quad\sqrt{\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}} &=\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}\\ \text{or}\quad\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}} &=\left(\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}\right)^{2} \\ &=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} N_{s 1} &=N_{s 2} \\ H_{1} &=H_{2} \\ \frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}} &=2 \end{aligned}\\ \text{We know that specific speed of the turbine,}\\ \begin{aligned} N_{s}&=\frac{N \sqrt{P}}{H^{5 / 4}}\\ \left(N_{s}\right)_{1} &=\left(N_{s}\right)_{2} \\ \frac{N_{1} \sqrt{P_{1}}}{H_{1}^{5 / 4}} &=\frac{N_{2} \sqrt{P_{2}}}{H_{2}^{5 / 4}} \\ N_{1} \sqrt{P_{1}} &=N_{2} \sqrt{P_{2}} \qquad\therefore H_{1}= h_{2} \\ \text{or}\quad\sqrt{\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}} &=\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}\\ \text{or}\quad\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}} &=\left(\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}\right)^{2} \\ &=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Under optimal conditions of the process the temperatures experienced by a copper work piece in fusion welding, brazing and soldering are such that
questions.explanation: In welding, the two metals (or thermoplastic) must be similar. For example, copper cannot be welded to steel. Welding uses high temperatures to melt and join two metal parts. A filler metal is often used as well. When properly done, the finished weld is as strong as the surrounding metal. Brazing joins two metals by heating and melting a filler (alloy) that bonds to the two pieces of metal and joins them. The filler obviously must have a melting temperature below that of the metal pieces. Brazing can join dissimilar metals such as aluminum, silver, copper, gold, and nickel. Soldering  is a low-temperature analog to brazing. By the American Welding Society’s definition, soldering takes place with fillers (also known as solders) that melt at below [latex]840^{\circ}F (450^{\circ}C)[/latex]. Metals that can be soldered include gold, silver, copper, brass, and iron. The filler, called solder, melts. When it solidifies, it is bonded to the metal parts and joins them. The bond is not as strong as brazed joint or welded one. Solder was once made mainly of lead, but environmental concerns are pushing industry to lead-free alternatives.
questions.explanation_html:
In welding, the two metals (or thermoplastic) must be similar. For example, copper cannot be welded to steel. Welding uses high temperatures to melt and join two metal parts. A filler metal is often used as well. When properly done, the finished weld is as strong as the surrounding metal.

Brazing joins two metals by heating and melting a filler (alloy) that bonds to the two pieces of metal and joins them. The filler obviously must have a melting temperature below that of the metal pieces. Brazing can join dissimilar metals such as aluminum, silver, copper, gold, and nickel.

Soldering is a low-temperature analog to brazing. By the American Welding Society’s definition, soldering takes place with fillers (also known as solders) that melt at below [latex]840^{\circ}F (450^{\circ}C)[/latex]. Metals that can be soldered include gold, silver, copper, brass, and iron. The filler, called solder, melts. When it solidifies, it is bonded to the metal parts and joins them. The bond is not as strong as brazed joint or welded one. Solder was once made mainly of lead, but environmental concerns are pushing industry to lead-free alternatives.

questions.question: Gauss-Seidel method is used to solve the following equations (as per the given order): [latex]x_{1}+2x_{2}+3x_{3}=5[/latex] [latex]2x_{1}+3x_{2}+x_{3}=1[/latex] [latex]3x_{1}+2x_{2}+x_{3}=3[/latex] Assuming initial guess as [latex]x_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}=0[/latex] , the value of [latex]x_{3}[/latex] after the first iteration is __________
questions.explanation: We are given: Initial guess: [latex] x_1^{(0)} = 0, , x_2^{(0)} = 0, , x_3^{(0)} = 0 [/latex]. We rewrite the equations for Gauss-Seidel iteration: From [latex] x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 5 [/latex]: [latex] x_1 = 5 - 2x_2 - 3x_3 [/latex] From [latex] 2x_1 + 3x_2 + x_3 = 1 [/latex]: [latex] x_2 = \frac{1 - 2x_1 - x_3}{3} [/latex] From [latex] 3x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 = 3 [/latex]: [latex] x_3 = 3 - 3x_1 - 2x_2 [/latex] First Iteration: Step 1: Compute [latex] x_1^{(1)} [/latex] Using [latex] x_2^{(0)} = 0 [/latex], [latex] x_3^{(0)} = 0 [/latex]: [latex] x_1^{(1)} = 5 - 2(0) - 3(0) = 5 [/latex] Step 2: Compute [latex] x_2^{(1)} [/latex] Using [latex] x_1^{(1)} = 5 [/latex], [latex] x_3^{(0)} = 0 [/latex]: [latex] x_2^{(1)} = \frac{1 - 2(5) - 0}{3} = \frac{1 - 10}{3} = \frac{-9}{3} = -3 [/latex] Step 3: Compute [latex] x_3^{(1)} [/latex] Using [latex] x_1^{(1)} = 5 [/latex], [latex] x_2^{(1)} = -3 [/latex]: [latex] x_3^{(1)} = 3 - 3(5) - 2(-3) = 3 - 15 + 6 = -6 [/latex] Final Answer: After the first iteration, [latex] x_3 = -6 [/latex].
questions.explanation_html:
We are given:
Initial guess: [latex] x_1^{(0)} = 0, , x_2^{(0)} = 0, , x_3^{(0)} = 0 [/latex].

We rewrite the equations for Gauss-Seidel iteration:
From [latex] x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 5 [/latex]:
[latex] x_1 = 5 - 2x_2 - 3x_3 [/latex]


From [latex] 2x_1 + 3x_2 + x_3 = 1 [/latex]:
[latex] x_2 = \frac{1 - 2x_1 - x_3}{3} [/latex]

From [latex] 3x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 = 3 [/latex]:
[latex] x_3 = 3 - 3x_1 - 2x_2 [/latex]

First Iteration:
Step 1:
Compute [latex] x_1^{(1)} [/latex]
Using [latex] x_2^{(0)} = 0 [/latex], [latex] x_3^{(0)} = 0 [/latex]:
[latex] x_1^{(1)} = 5 - 2(0) - 3(0) = 5 [/latex]

Step 2: Compute [latex] x_2^{(1)} [/latex]
Using [latex] x_1^{(1)} = 5 [/latex], [latex] x_3^{(0)} = 0 [/latex]:
[latex] x_2^{(1)} = \frac{1 - 2(5) - 0}{3} = \frac{1 - 10}{3} = \frac{-9}{3} = -3 [/latex]

Step 3: Compute [latex] x_3^{(1)} [/latex]
Using [latex] x_1^{(1)} = 5 [/latex], [latex] x_2^{(1)} = -3 [/latex]:
[latex] x_3^{(1)} = 3 - 3(5) - 2(-3) = 3 - 15 + 6 = -6 [/latex]

Final Answer: After the first iteration, [latex] x_3 = -6 [/latex].

questions.question: A block of mass m rests on an inclined plane and is attached by a string to the wall as shown in the figure. The coefficient of static friction between the plane and the block is 0.25. The string can withstand a maximum force of 20 N. The maximum value of the mass (m) for which the string will not break and the block will be in static equilibrium is ____________ kg. Take [latex]\cos\theta =0.8[/latex]  and [latex]\sin\theta =0.6[/latex] Acceleration due to gravity [latex]g=10m/s^{2}[/latex]
questions.explanation: [latex]M_{\text {static }} =0.25 [/latex] [latex] F_{max} =20 \mathrm{N}[/latex] Balancing force along the inclined plane [latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad T+f&=m g \sin \theta \\ f &=\mu \mathrm{N} \\ N &=m g \cos \theta \end{aligned} [/latex] (balancing forces perpendicular to the inclined plane) [latex] 20+0.25 \times m g \cos \theta=m g \sin \theta [/latex] [latex] 20+0.25 \times m \times 10 \times 0.8=m \times 10 \times 0.6 [/latex] [latex] 20=4 m [/latex] [latex] \therefore \quad m=5 \mathrm{kg}[/latex]
questions.topic: FBD, Equilirbium, Plane Trusses and Virtual work
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]M_{\text {static }} =0.25 [/latex]
[latex] F_{max} =20 \mathrm{N}[/latex]


Balancing force along the inclined plane
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad T+f&=m g \sin \theta \\ f &=\mu \mathrm{N} \\ N &=m g \cos \theta \end{aligned} [/latex]
(balancing forces perpendicular to the inclined plane)
[latex] 20+0.25 \times m g \cos \theta=m g \sin \theta [/latex]
[latex] 20+0.25 \times m \times 10 \times 0.8=m \times 10 \times 0.6 [/latex]
[latex] 20=4 m [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad m=5 \mathrm{kg}[/latex]

questions.question: A simply-supported beam of length 3L is subjected to the loading shown in the figure. It is given that P = 1 N, L = 1 m and Young's modulus E = 200 GPa. The cross-section is a square with dimension 10 mm x 10 mm. questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \Sigma F_{V} &=0 \\ R_{1}+R_{2} &=0 \\ \Sigma M_{1} &=0 \\ 3 R_{2} L-2 P L+P L &=0 \\ R_{2} &=\frac{P}{3} \\ R_{1} &=\frac{-P}{3}\\ \mathrm{B.M} \text { at } A,\; M_{A}&=\left(R_{1} \times 1.5 L\right)+(P \times 0.5 L) \\ &=\left(\frac{-P}{3} \times 1.5 L\right)+0.5 P L=0\\ \therefore \text{B.M. at A} &= 0\\ \therefore \text{Bending stress }&= 0\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \Sigma F_{V} &=0 \\ R_{1}+R_{2} &=0 \\ \Sigma M_{1} &=0 \\ 3 R_{2} L-2 P L+P L &=0 \\ R_{2} &=\frac{P}{3} \\ R_{1} &=\frac{-P}{3}\\ \mathrm{B.M} \text { at } A,\; M_{A}&=\left(R_{1} \times 1.5 L\right)+(P \times 0.5 L) \\ &=\left(\frac{-P}{3} \times 1.5 L\right)+0.5 P L=0\\ \therefore \text{B.M. at A} &= 0\\ \therefore \text{Bending stress }&= 0\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: In the gear train shown, gear 3 is carried on arm 5. Gear 3 meshes with gear 2 and gear 4. The number of teeth on gear 2, 3, and 4 are 60, 20, and 100, respectively. If gear 2 is fixed and gear 4 rotates with an angular velocity of 100 rpm in the counterclockwise direction, the angular speed of arm 5 (in rpm) is
questions.explanation: Given : Gear 2 is fixed [latex] \therefore \quad N+y=0 \qquad [\therefore N=-y][/latex] Gear 4 rotates 100 rpm is counter clockwise. [latex] \begin{aligned} -\frac{N \times 60}{100}+y &=-100 \\ +y \times 0.6+y &=-100 \\ y &=\frac{-100}{1.6}=-62.5 \end{aligned}[/latex] Hence angular speed of arm is 62.5 (counterclockwise).

Given : Gear 2 is fixed

Hence angular speed of arm is 62.5
(counterclockwise).

questions.question:
A solid disc with radius a is connected to a spring at a point d above the center of the disc. The other end of the spring is fixed to the vertical wall. The disc is free to roll without slipping on the
ground. The mass of the disc is M and the spring constant is K. The polar moment of inertia for the
disc about its centre is [latex]J=Ma^{2}/2[/latex] The natural frequency of this system in rad/s is given by
questions.explanation: Total energy of system [latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} M v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K x^{2}+\frac{1}{2} I \omega^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} M \times\left(a \times \frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times \\ \qquad \{(a+d) \theta\}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{M a^{2}}{2} \times\left(\frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}\\ \text{Let}\qquad \frac{d \theta}{d t}=\dot{\theta} \\ E=\frac{1}{2} M a^{2} \dot{\theta}^{2}+\frac{K}{2}(a+d)^{2} \cdot \theta^{2}+\frac{M a^{2}}{4} \dot{\theta}^{2} \end{array}[/latex] since energy of system remains concerned with respect to time. [latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d E}{d t}&=0 \\ \frac{d E}{d t}&=\frac{M a^{2}}{2} 2 \cdot \dot{\theta} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+\frac{K}{2}(a+d)^{2} \\ & \qquad \cdot 2 \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M a^{2}}{4} \cdot 2 \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]0=M a^{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{\lt a^{2}}{2} \cdot \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}[/latex] Divide both sides by [latex]\dot{\theta} [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} 0&=M a^{2} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{M a^{2}}{2} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \cdot \theta \\ 0&=\left(M a^{2}+\frac{M a^{2}}{2}\right) \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \\ 0&=\frac{3}{2} M a^{2} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \end{aligned}[/latex] Divide both sides by [latex] \frac{3}{2} m a^{2} [/latex] [latex] 0=\ddot{\theta}+\frac{K(a+d)^{2}}{\frac{3 M a^{2}}{2}} \theta[/latex] [latex] \ddot{\theta}+\omega_{n}^{2} \theta=0[/latex] Compairing above two equation [latex] \omega_{n}^{2}=\frac{2 K(a+d)^{2}}{3 M a^{2}} ; \omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{2 K(a+d)^{2}}{3 M a^{2}}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Total energy of system
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} M v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K x^{2}+\frac{1}{2} I \omega^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} M \times\left(a \times \frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times \\ \qquad \{(a+d) \theta\}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{M a^{2}}{2} \times\left(\frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}\\ \text{Let}\qquad \frac{d \theta}{d t}=\dot{\theta} \\ E=\frac{1}{2} M a^{2} \dot{\theta}^{2}+\frac{K}{2}(a+d)^{2} \cdot \theta^{2}+\frac{M a^{2}}{4} \dot{\theta}^{2} \end{array}[/latex]
since energy of system remains concerned with
respect to time.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d E}{d t}&=0 \\ \frac{d E}{d t}&=\frac{M a^{2}}{2} 2 \cdot \dot{\theta} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+\frac{K}{2}(a+d)^{2} \\ & \qquad \cdot 2 \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M a^{2}}{4} \cdot 2 \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]0=M a^{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{\lt a^{2}}{2} \cdot \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}[/latex]
Divide both sides by [latex]\dot{\theta} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} 0&=M a^{2} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{M a^{2}}{2} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \cdot \theta \\ 0&=\left(M a^{2}+\frac{M a^{2}}{2}\right) \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \\ 0&=\frac{3}{2} M a^{2} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \end{aligned}[/latex]
Divide both sides by [latex] \frac{3}{2} m a^{2} [/latex]
[latex] 0=\ddot{\theta}+\frac{K(a+d)^{2}}{\frac{3 M a^{2}}{2}} \theta[/latex]
[latex] \ddot{\theta}+\omega_{n}^{2} \theta=0[/latex]
Compairing above two equation
[latex] \omega_{n}^{2}=\frac{2 K(a+d)^{2}}{3 M a^{2}} ; \omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{2 K(a+d)^{2}}{3 M a^{2}}}[/latex]

questions.question: The principal stresses at a point inside a solid object are [latex]\sigma _{1}=100[/latex]  Mpa, [latex]\sigma _{2}=100[/latex] MPa and [latex]\sigma _{3}=0[/latex] Mpa.  The yield strength of the material is 200 MPa. The factor of safety calculated using Tresca (maximum shear stress) theory is [latex]n_{T}[/latex] and the factor of safety calculated using von Mises (maximum distortional energy) theory is [latex]n_{V}[/latex]. Which one of the following relations is TRUE?
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{array}{l} \sigma_{1}=100 \mathrm{MPa}, \sigma_{2}=100 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{3}=0 \\ \sigma_{y}=200 \mathrm{MPa} \end{array}[/latex] According to Tresca theory [latex] \begin{aligned} \tau_{\max } & \leq \frac{\sigma_{y}}{2 F O S} \\ \tau_{\max } &=\frac{\sigma_{y}}{2 n_{T}} \\ \text{now}\quad \tau_{\max _{\mathrm{abs}}} &=\frac{\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{3}}{2}=50 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \therefore \quad 50 &=\frac{200}{2 n_{T}}\\ \therefore \quad n_{T}&=2 \end{aligned}[/latex] According to Von-Mises theory [latex] \begin{array}{l} \sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}-\sigma_{1} \sigma_{2} \leq\left(\frac{\sigma_{y}}{n_{V}}\right)^{2} \\ 100^{2}+100^{2}-100 \times 100 \leq\left(\frac{200}{n_{V}}\right)^{2} \\ \therefore \quad 100=\frac{200}{n_{v}}\\ \text{or}\quad n_{v}=2 \end{array}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} \sigma_{1}=100 \mathrm{MPa}, \sigma_{2}=100 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \sigma_{3}=0 \\ \sigma_{y}=200 \mathrm{MPa} \end{array}[/latex]
According to Tresca theory
[latex] \begin{aligned} \tau_{\max } & \leq \frac{\sigma_{y}}{2 F O S} \\ \tau_{\max } &=\frac{\sigma_{y}}{2 n_{T}} \\ \text{now}\quad \tau_{\max _{\mathrm{abs}}} &=\frac{\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{3}}{2}=50 \mathrm{MPa} \\ \therefore \quad 50 &=\frac{200}{2 n_{T}}\\ \therefore \quad n_{T}&=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
According to Von-Mises theory
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}-\sigma_{1} \sigma_{2} \leq\left(\frac{\sigma_{y}}{n_{V}}\right)^{2} \\ 100^{2}+100^{2}-100 \times 100 \leq\left(\frac{200}{n_{V}}\right)^{2} \\ \therefore \quad 100=\frac{200}{n_{v}}\\ \text{or}\quad n_{v}=2 \end{array}[/latex]

questions.question: An inverted U-tube manometer is used to measure the pressure difference between two pipes A and B, as shown in the figure. Pipe A is carrying oil (specific gravity = 0.8) and pipe B is carrying water. The densities of air and water are 1.16kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex]  and 1000kg/[latex]m^{3}[/latex], respectively. The pressure difference between pipes A and B is __________kPa. Acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/[latex]s^{2}[/latex] .
questions.explanation: Given data: Specific gravity of oil, [latex] s^{oil} = 0.8[/latex] [latex] \therefore \quad \rho_{\mathrm{oil}}=0.8 \times 1000=800 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex] Density of air: [latex]\rho_{\text {air }}=1.16 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex] Density of water, [latex] \rho_{\text {water }}=1000 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex] Acceleration due to gravity, [latex] \begin{aligned} g &=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} \\ h_{1} &=80 \mathrm{mm}=0.08 \mathrm{m} \\ h_{2} &=200 \mathrm{mm}=0.2 \mathrm{m} \\ h_{3} &=100 \mathrm{mm}=0.1 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex] Pressure at section 1 on left limb = Pressure at section 1 on right limb [latex] \begin{aligned} P_{A}-\rho_{\text {oil }} g h_{2}-\rho_{\text {air }} g h_{1}&=p_{B}-\rho_{\text {water }} g\left(h_{1}+h_{2}+h_{3})\right. \\ p_{A}-800 \times 10 \times 0.2&-1.16 \times 10 \times 0.08 =p_{B}-\\ &1000 \times 10(0.08+0.2+0.1) \\ p_{A}-1600-0.928&=p_{B}-3800\\ p_{A}-p_{B} &=-2199.07 \mathrm{Pa} \\ &=-2.199 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given data:
Specific gravity of oil,
[latex] s^{oil} = 0.8[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \rho_{\mathrm{oil}}=0.8 \times 1000=800 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]
Density of air: [latex]\rho_{\text {air }}=1.16 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex]
Density of water,
[latex] \rho_{\text {water }}=1000 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex]
Acceleration due to gravity,
[latex] \begin{aligned} g &=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} \\ h_{1} &=80 \mathrm{mm}=0.08 \mathrm{m} \\ h_{2} &=200 \mathrm{mm}=0.2 \mathrm{m} \\ h_{3} &=100 \mathrm{mm}=0.1 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Pressure at section 1 on left limb = Pressure at
section 1 on right limb
[latex] \begin{aligned} P_{A}-\rho_{\text {oil }} g h_{2}-\rho_{\text {air }} g h_{1}&=p_{B}-\rho_{\text {water }} g\left(h_{1}+h_{2}+h_{3})\right. \\ p_{A}-800 \times 10 \times 0.2&-1.16 \times 10 \times 0.08 =p_{B}-\\ &1000 \times 10(0.08+0.2+0.1) \\ p_{A}-1600-0.928&=p_{B}-3800\\ p_{A}-p_{B} &=-2199.07 \mathrm{Pa} \\ &=-2.199 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
Oil (kinematic viscosity, [latex]v_{oil}=1.0\times 10^{-5}m^{2}/s[/latex] ) flows through a pipe of 0.5 m diameter with a velocity of 10 m/s. Water (kinematic viscosity,[latex]v_{w}=0.89\times 10^{-6}m^{2}/s[/latex] ) is flowing through a model
pipe of diameter 20 mm. For satisfying the dynamic similarity, the velocity of water (in m/s)
is __________
questions.explanation: Given data: For prototype [latex] \begin{aligned} v_{p}&=1.0 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \\ d_{p}&=0.5 \mathrm{m} \\ V_{p}&=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}\\ \text{For model}\\ v_{m}&=0.89 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \\ d_{m}&=20 \mathrm{mm}=0.02 \mathrm{m} \\ V_{m}&=? \end{aligned}[/latex] We know that Reynolds number, [latex] \begin{aligned} Re &=\frac{V d}{v} \\ (R e)_{m} &=(R e)_{p} \\ \frac{V_{m} d_{m}}{v_{m}} &=\frac{V_{p} d_{p}}{v_{p}} \\ \frac{V_{m} \times 0.02}{0.89 \times 10^{-6}} &=\frac{10 \times 0.5}{1.0 \times 10^{-5}} \\ \text{or }\quad V_{m} &=22.25 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex] or The velocity of water is [latex]22.25 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}[/latex]

questions.question: A steady laminar boundary layer is formed over a flat plate as shown in the figure. The free stream velocity of the fluid is [latex]U_{0}[/latex]. The velocity profile at the inlet a-b is uniform, while that at a downstream location c-d is given by [latex]u=U_{0}\left [ 2( \frac{y}{\delta }) -(\frac{y}\delta {})^{2}\right ][/latex] . The ratio of the mass flow rate, [latex]\dot{m}_{bd}[/latex]  leaving through the horizontal section b-d to that entering through the vertical section a-b is ___________
questions.explanation: [latex] U_{0}= [/latex] Velocity of free stream d= Boundary layer thickness at section c-d b= Width of the plate Velocity profile, [latex] u=U_{0}\left[2\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)-\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)^{2}\right][/latex] Mass flow rate through section a-b, [latex] \begin{aligned} \dot{m}_{\mathrm{ab}} &=\rho A U_{0} \\ &=\rho b \delta U_{0} \end{aligned}[/latex] Mass flow rate through section c-d [latex] \dot{m}_{c d}=\int_{0}^{\delta} \rho b d y U[/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{\delta} \rho b U_{0}\left[2 \frac{y}{\delta}-\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)^{2}\right] d y \\ m_{c d} &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\frac{2 y^{2}}{2 \delta}-\frac{y^{3}}{3 \delta^{2}}\right]_{0}^{\delta}\\ &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta}-\frac{\delta^{3}}{3 \delta^{2}}\right]\\ &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\delta-\frac{\delta}{3}\right] \\ &=\rho b U_{0} \times \frac{2}{3} \delta \\ &=\frac{2}{3} \rho b \delta U_{0}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Mass flow rate through section b-d, [latex]\begin{aligned} \dot{m_{bd}} &=\dot{m_{ad}}- \dot{m_{cd}} \\ &= \rho b\delta U_0-\frac{2}{3}\rho b\delta U_0\\ &= \frac{\rho b\delta U_0}{3}\\ \frac{\dot{m_{bd}}}{\dot{m_{ab}}}&=\frac{\rho b\delta U_0}{3 \times \rho b\delta U_0}=\frac{1}{3}=0.333 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.explanation_html:
[latex] U_{0}= [/latex] Velocity of free stream
d= Boundary layer thickness at section c-d
b= Width of the plate
Velocity profile,
[latex] u=U_{0}\left[2\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)-\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)^{2}\right][/latex]
Mass flow rate through section a-b,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \dot{m}_{\mathrm{ab}} &=\rho A U_{0} \\ &=\rho b \delta U_{0} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Mass flow rate through section c-d
[latex] \dot{m}_{c d}=\int_{0}^{\delta} \rho b d y U[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{\delta} \rho b U_{0}\left[2 \frac{y}{\delta}-\left(\frac{y}{\delta}\right)^{2}\right] d y \\ m_{c d} &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\frac{2 y^{2}}{2 \delta}-\frac{y^{3}}{3 \delta^{2}}\right]_{0}^{\delta}\\ &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta}-\frac{\delta^{3}}{3 \delta^{2}}\right]\\ &=\rho b U_{0}\left[\delta-\frac{\delta}{3}\right] \\ &=\rho b U_{0} \times \frac{2}{3} \delta \\ &=\frac{2}{3} \rho b \delta U_{0}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Mass flow rate through section b-d,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \dot{m_{bd}} &=\dot{m_{ad}}- \dot{m_{cd}} \\ &= \rho b\delta U_0-\frac{2}{3}\rho b\delta U_0\\ &= \frac{\rho b\delta U_0}{3}\\ \frac{\dot{m_{bd}}}{\dot{m_{ab}}}&=\frac{\rho b\delta U_0}{3 \times \rho b\delta U_0}=\frac{1}{3}=0.333 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: A steel ball of 10 mm diameter at 1000 K is required to be cooled to 350 K by immersing it in a water environment at 300 K. The convective heat transfer coefficient is 1000 [latex]W/m^{2}-K[/latex]  Thermal conductivity of steel is 40 W/m-K. The time constant for the cooling process [latex]\tau[/latex]  is 16 s. The time required (in s) to reach the final temperature is __________
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Diameter of ball } &=10 \mathrm{mm} \\ T_{\text {initial }} &=1000 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{\text {final }} &=350 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{\infty} &=300 \mathrm{K} \\ h &=1000 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \\ k &=40 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ \text { Time constant } &=16 \mathrm{s} \\ \text { Time required } &=t \mathrm{s} \\ \frac{T-T_{\infty}}{T_{i}-T_{\infty}} &=e^{-\frac{h A t}{\rho v c}} \\ &=16 \mathrm{second} \\ \text { But } \quad \frac{\rho v c}{h A} &=\text { Time constant } \\ \frac{350-300}{1000-300} &=e^{-\frac{1}{16}} \times t \\ 0.07143 &=e^{-t/ 16} \end{aligned}[/latex] Taking [latex] \log _{e} [/latex] both sides, we get [latex] \begin{aligned} \log _{e} 0.07143 &=\frac{-t}{16} \log _{e} e & &\left(\because \log _{e} e=1\right) \\ -2.639 &= \frac{-t}{16} \\ \text{or}\quad t &=42.23 \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Diameter of ball } &=10 \mathrm{mm} \\ T_{\text {initial }} &=1000 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{\text {final }} &=350 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{\infty} &=300 \mathrm{K} \\ h &=1000 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \\ k &=40 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \\ \text { Time constant } &=16 \mathrm{s} \\ \text { Time required } &=t \mathrm{s} \\ \frac{T-T_{\infty}}{T_{i}-T_{\infty}} &=e^{-\frac{h A t}{\rho v c}} \\ &=16 \mathrm{second} \\ \text { But } \quad \frac{\rho v c}{h A} &=\text { Time constant } \\ \frac{350-300}{1000-300} &=e^{-\frac{1}{16}} \times t \\ 0.07143 &=e^{-t/ 16} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking [latex] \log _{e} [/latex] both sides, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \log _{e} 0.07143 &=\frac{-t}{16} \log _{e} e & &\left(\because \log _{e} e=1\right) \\ -2.639 &= \frac{-t}{16} \\ \text{or}\quad t &=42.23 \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The view factor, [latex]F_{1-2}[/latex]  is 0.26. The net radiation heat loss or gain on side 1 is_________ W/m. Stefan-Boltzmann constant = [latex]5.67\times10 ^{-8}W/m^{2}-k^{4}[/latex]

questions.question: A fluid (Prandtl number, Pr = 1) at 500 K flows over a flat plate of 1.5 m length, maintained at 300 K. The velocity of the fluid is 10 m/s. Assuming kinematic viscosity, v=30 [latex]\times 10^{-6}m^{2}/s[/latex],  the thermal boundary layer thickness (in mm) at 0.5 m from the leading edge is __________
questions.explanation: Given [latex] \begin{aligned} P r &=1 \\ T_{\infty} &=500 \mathrm{K} \\ \text { Length } &=1.5 \mathrm{m} \\ T_{\text {plate }} &=300 \mathrm{K} \\ U_{\infty} &=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ v &=30 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex] Thermal boundary layer at [latex]0.5 \mathrm{m}[/latex] from leadra edge [latex] =\delta_{t} [/latex] [latex] \text{Re}_{x=0.5}=\frac{U x}{v}=\frac{10 \times 0.5}{30 \times 10^{-6}}=166,666.67 [/latex] since [latex] \text{Re}_{x=0.5} \lt 5 \times 10^{5}[/latex]. Hence flow is laminar [latex] \begin{aligned}\therefore \quad \delta &=\frac{5 x}{\sqrt{\text{Re}_{x}}} \\ &=\frac{5 \times 0.5}{\sqrt{166,666.67}} \\ &=6.1237 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ \frac{\delta_{t}}{\delta} &=\left(P_{f}\right)^{1 / 3} \\ \delta_{t} &=(1)^{1 / 3} \times \delta \\ &=1 \times 6.1237 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ &=6.1237 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Given
[latex] \begin{aligned} P r &=1 \\ T_{\infty} &=500 \mathrm{K} \\ \text { Length } &=1.5 \mathrm{m} \\ T_{\text {plate }} &=300 \mathrm{K} \\ U_{\infty} &=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ v &=30 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thermal boundary layer at [latex]0.5 \mathrm{m}[/latex] from leadra edge [latex] =\delta_{t} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Re}_{x=0.5}=\frac{U x}{v}=\frac{10 \times 0.5}{30 \times 10^{-6}}=166,666.67 [/latex]
since [latex] \text{Re}_{x=0.5} \lt 5 \times 10^{5}[/latex]. Hence flow is laminar
[latex] \begin{aligned}\therefore \quad \delta &=\frac{5 x}{\sqrt{\text{Re}_{x}}} \\ &=\frac{5 \times 0.5}{\sqrt{166,666.67}} \\ &=6.1237 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ \frac{\delta_{t}}{\delta} &=\left(P_{f}\right)^{1 / 3} \\ \delta_{t} &=(1)^{1 / 3} \times \delta \\ &=1 \times 6.1237 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ &=6.1237 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: In a steam power plant operating on an ideal Rankine cycle, superheated steam enters the turbine at 3  MPa  and [latex]350^{\circ}C[/latex] .The condenser pressure is 75 kPa. The thermal efficiency of the cycle is ________ percent. Given data: For saturated liquid, at P = 75 kPa. [latex]h_{f}=384.39[/latex]  kJ/kg, [latex]v_{f}=0.001037 m^{3}/kg[/latex]  , [latex]s_{f}=1.213[/latex]  kJ/kg-K At 75 kPa, [latex]h_{fg}[/latex] =2278.6 kJ/kg,[latex]s_{fg}[/latex] =6.2434 kJ/kg-K At P = 3 MPa and T = [latex]350^{\circ}C[/latex]  (superheated steam), h = 3115.3kJ/kg, s = 6.7428 kJ/kg-K
questions.explanation: Calculating dryness fraction at point 2 [latex] \begin{aligned} S_{1} &=S_{2} \\ 6.7248 &=s_{f}+x_{2} s_{f g} \\ &=1.213+x_{2} \times 6.2434 \\ x_{2} &=\frac{6.7428-1.213}{6.2434}\\ &=0.8857 \end{aligned}[/latex] Calculating enthalpy at point 2 [latex] \begin{aligned} h_{2} &=h_{f}+x_{2} h_{f g} \\ &=384.39+0.8857 \times 2278.6 \\ &=2402.546 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \text { Given: } \quad h_{1} &=3115.3 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ h_{4} &=h_{3}+v d P \\ &=384.39+0.001037 \times[3000-75] \\ &=387.423 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \text { Pump work } &=v d P \\ &=0.001037 \times[3000-75] \\ &=3.033 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ w_{\text {net }} &=w_{T}-w_{P}=\left(h_{1}-h_{2}\right)-3.033 \\ &=(3115.3-2402.546)-3.033 \\ &=709.721 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}\\ \text{Heat input }&=h_{1}-h_{4}\\ &=3115.3-387.423 \\ &=2727.877 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}\\ \text{Efficiency of cycle }&=\frac{\text { Work delivered }}{\text { Heat input }} \\ & \frac{709.721}{2727877} \\ &=0.2601=26.01 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Calculating dryness fraction at point 2
[latex] \begin{aligned} S_{1} &=S_{2} \\ 6.7248 &=s_{f}+x_{2} s_{f g} \\ &=1.213+x_{2} \times 6.2434 \\ x_{2} &=\frac{6.7428-1.213}{6.2434}\\ &=0.8857 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Calculating enthalpy at point 2
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_{2} &=h_{f}+x_{2} h_{f g} \\ &=384.39+0.8857 \times 2278.6 \\ &=2402.546 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \text { Given: } \quad h_{1} &=3115.3 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ h_{4} &=h_{3}+v d P \\ &=384.39+0.001037 \times[3000-75] \\ &=387.423 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \text { Pump work } &=v d P \\ &=0.001037 \times[3000-75] \\ &=3.033 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ w_{\text {net }} &=w_{T}-w_{P}=\left(h_{1}-h_{2}\right)-3.033 \\ &=(3115.3-2402.546)-3.033 \\ &=709.721 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}\\ \text{Heat input }&=h_{1}-h_{4}\\ &=3115.3-387.423 \\ &=2727.877 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}\\ \text{Efficiency of cycle }&=\frac{\text { Work delivered }}{\text { Heat input }} \\ & \frac{709.721}{2727877} \\ &=0.2601=26.01 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider the radiation heat exchange inside an annulus between two very long concentric cylinders. The radius of the outer cylinder is [latex]R_{0}[/latex]  and that of the inner cylinder is [latex]R_{i}[/latex] . The radiation view factor of the outer cylinder onto itself is
questions.explanation: To find: Radiation view factor of the outer cylinder onto itself. Hence [latex] F_{11} [/latex] is required. [latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow A_{1} F_{12}&=A_{2} F_{21} \qquad[\text { Reciprosity }]\\ F_{11}+F_{12}&=1 \qquad \text { [Summation] }\\ F_{21}+F_{22}&=1\\ \therefore \quad F_{11}&=1-F_{12} \\ F_{22}&=0  \text { [No radiation leaving }\\ &\text{surface 2 reaches back to 2]}\\ \therefore \quad F_{21} &=1 \\ F_{12} &=\frac{A_{2}}{A_{1}} \times F_{21}=\frac{A_{2}}{A_{1}} \times 1 \\ &=\frac{2 \pi R_{i} L}{2 \pi R_{0} L} \times 1=\frac{R_{i}}{R_{0}} \\ F_{11} &=1-F_{12}=1-\frac{R_{i}}{R_{0}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
To find: Radiation view factor of the outer cylinder onto itself.
Hence [latex] F_{11} [/latex] is required.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow A_{1} F_{12}&=A_{2} F_{21} \qquad[\text { Reciprosity }]\\ F_{11}+F_{12}&=1 \qquad \text { [Summation] }\\ F_{21}+F_{22}&=1\\ \therefore \quad F_{11}&=1-F_{12} \\ F_{22}&=0 \text { [No radiation leaving }\\ &\text{surface 2 reaches back to 2]}\\ \therefore \quad F_{21} &=1 \\ F_{12} &=\frac{A_{2}}{A_{1}} \times F_{21}=\frac{A_{2}}{A_{1}} \times 1 \\ &=\frac{2 \pi R_{i} L}{2 \pi R_{0} L} \times 1=\frac{R_{i}}{R_{0}} \\ F_{11} &=1-F_{12}=1-\frac{R_{i}}{R_{0}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider a simple gas turbine (Brayton) cycle and a gas turbine cycle with perfect regeneration. [latex] \frac{T_{\max }}{T_{\min }}=0.3 \quad[/latex] [for regenerative cycle ]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \eta_\text { Tregenerative cycle } &=1-\frac{T_{\max }}{T_{\min }} \times\left(r_{p}\right)^{(\gamma-1) / \gamma} \\ &=1-0.3\times(6)^{\frac{0.4}{1.4}}\\ &=0.49945 \times(6)^{\frac{0.4}{1.4}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \eta_{\text {simplecycle }} &=1-\frac{1}{\left(r_{p}\right)^{(\gamma-1) / \gamma}} \\ &=1-\left(r_{p}\right)^{(1-\gamma) / \gamma} \\ &=1-(6)^{-\frac{0.4}{1.4}}=0.4066 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Required ratio } &=\frac{\eta_{\text {simple cycle }}}{\eta_{\text {regenerative cycle }}} \\ &=\frac{0.40666}{0.49945}=0.8141 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: The system shown in the figure consists of block A of mass 5 kg connected to a spring through a massless rope passing over pulley B of radius r and mass 20 kg. The spring constant k is 1500 N/m. If there is no slipping of the rope over the pulley, the natural frequency of the system is_____________ rad/s.
questions.explanation: Total energy of system [latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} k x^{2}+\frac{1}{2} I \omega^{2} \\ &=\frac{1}{2} m\left(r \times \frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times(r \theta)^{2} \\&+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{M r^{2}}{2} \times\left[\frac{d \theta}{d T}\right]^{2} \\ &=\frac{1}{2} M r^{2} \cdot(\dot{\theta})^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times r^{2} \theta^{2}+\frac{M r^{2}}{4}(\dot{\theta})^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] since total energy remains constant with respect to time. [latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d E}{d t} &=0 \\ \frac{d E}{d t} &=\frac{1}{2} m r^{2} 2 \cdot \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{K r^{2}}{2} \cdot 2 \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M r^{2}}{4} 2 \dot{\theta} \dot{\theta} \\ 0 &=m r^{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+K r^{2} \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M r^{2}}{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta} \end{aligned}[/latex] Divide both sides by [latex]\dot{\theta} [/latex] [latex] 0=m r^{2} \ddot{\theta}+K r^{2} \theta+\frac{M r^{2}}{2}[/latex] Divide both sides by [latex]r^{2} [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} 0 &=m \ddot{\theta}+K \theta+\frac{M \ddot{\theta}}{2} \\ 0 &=\left(m+\frac{M}{2}\right) \ddot{\theta}+K \theta \\ 0 &=\ddot{\theta}+\left[\frac{K}{m+\frac{M}{2}}\right] \theta \\ \omega_{n}^{2} &=\frac{K}{m+\frac{M}{2}} \\ \omega_{n} &=\sqrt{\frac{2 k}{M+2 m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1500}{20+(2 \times 5)}} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{3000}{20+10}}=\sqrt{100} \\ &=10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Total energy of system
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} k x^{2}+\frac{1}{2} I \omega^{2} \\ &=\frac{1}{2} m\left(r \times \frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times(r \theta)^{2} \\&+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{M r^{2}}{2} \times\left[\frac{d \theta}{d T}\right]^{2} \\ &=\frac{1}{2} M r^{2} \cdot(\dot{\theta})^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times r^{2} \theta^{2}+\frac{M r^{2}}{4}(\dot{\theta})^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
since total energy remains constant with respect to time.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d E}{d t} &=0 \\ \frac{d E}{d t} &=\frac{1}{2} m r^{2} 2 \cdot \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{K r^{2}}{2} \cdot 2 \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M r^{2}}{4} 2 \dot{\theta} \dot{\theta} \\ 0 &=m r^{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+K r^{2} \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M r^{2}}{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Divide both sides by [latex]\dot{\theta} [/latex]
[latex] 0=m r^{2} \ddot{\theta}+K r^{2} \theta+\frac{M r^{2}}{2}[/latex]
Divide both sides by [latex]r^{2} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} 0 &=m \ddot{\theta}+K \theta+\frac{M \ddot{\theta}}{2} \\ 0 &=\left(m+\frac{M}{2}\right) \ddot{\theta}+K \theta \\ 0 &=\ddot{\theta}+\left[\frac{K}{m+\frac{M}{2}}\right] \theta \\ \omega_{n}^{2} &=\frac{K}{m+\frac{M}{2}} \\ \omega_{n} &=\sqrt{\frac{2 k}{M+2 m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1500}{20+(2 \times 5)}} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{3000}{20+10}}=\sqrt{100} \\ &=10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: In a structural member under fatigue loading, the minimum and maximum stresses developed at the critical point are 50 MPaand 150 MParespectively. questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned}  \sigma _{max}&=150MPa\\ \sigma _{min}&=50MPa\\ S_e&=200MPa\\ S_{yt}&=300MPa\\ S_{ut}&=400MPa\\ \sigma _a&=\frac{\sigma _{max}-\sigma _{min}}{2}\\ &=\frac{150-50}{2}\\ &=50 MPa\\ \sigma _m&=\frac{\sigma _{max}+\sigma _{min}}{2}\\ &=\frac{150+50}{2}\\ &=100 MPa\\ &\text{Goodman sequation}\\ \frac{\sigma _a}{S_e}+\frac{\sigma _m}{S_{ut}}&=\frac{1}{FS}\\ \frac{50}{200}+\frac{100}{400}&=\frac{1}{FS}\\ FS&=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Two cylindrical shafts A and B at the same initial temperature are simultaneously placed in a furnace. The surfaces of the shafts remain at the furnace gas temperature at all times after they are introduced into the furnace. The temperature variation in the axial direction of the shafts can be assumed to be negligible. The data related to shafts A and B is given in the following Table. The temperature at the centerline of the shaft A reaches [latex]400^{\circ}[/latex] C after two hours. The time required (in hours) for the centerline of the shaft B to attain the temperature of [latex]400^{\circ}[/latex] C is _______
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} T_{(r, t)} &=T_{0}+\left(T_{\infty}-T_{0}\right) \operatorname{erf}(z) \\ \frac{T_{(r, t)}-T_{0}}{T_{\infty}-T_{0}} &=\operatorname{erf}(z) \\ \frac{T_{(r, t)}-T_{0}}{T_{\infty}-T_{0}} &=\operatorname{erf}(z) \end{aligned}[/latex] For shaft A [latex]\quad \frac{T_{0.2, t}-T_{i}}{400-T_{i}} [/latex] For shaft B [latex]\quad \frac{T_{0.05, t}-T_{i}}{400-T_{i}} [/latex] Hence error function of both shafts will be same. [latex] \therefore \qquad z_{A}=z_{B}[/latex][latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{\Gamma_{A}}{2 \sqrt{\alpha_{A} t_{A}}} &=\frac{T_{B}}{2 \sqrt{\alpha_{B} t_{B}}} \\ \frac{\Gamma_{A}}{\sqrt{\alpha_{A} t_{A}}} &=\frac{\Gamma_{B}}{\sqrt{\alpha_{B} t_{B}}} \\ \frac{\Gamma_{A}^{2}}{\alpha_{A} t_{A}} &=\frac{r_{B}^{2}}{\alpha_{B} t_{B}} \\ t_{B} &=\left(\frac{r_{B}}{r_{A}}\right)^{2} \times \frac{\alpha_{A}}{\alpha_{B}} \times t_{A} \\ \alpha_{A} &=\frac{k}{\rho c_{p}}=\frac{40}{2 \times 10^{6}}=\frac{20}{10^{6}} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \\ \alpha_{B} &=\frac{k}{\rho c_{p}}=\frac{20}{2 \times 10^{7}}=\frac{1}{10^{6}} \mathrm{m}^{2} / \mathrm{s} \\ t_{B} &=\left(\frac{r_{B}}{r_{A}}\right)^{2} \times \frac{\alpha_{A}}{\alpha_{B}} \times t_{A} \\ &=\left(\frac{0.1}{0.4}\right)^{2} \times \frac{20}{10^{6} \times \frac{1}{10^{6}}} \times 2 \\ &=\frac{1}{16} \times 20 \times 2=2.5 \mathrm{hrs} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
The partial pressure of water vapour in a moist air sample of relative humidity 70% is 1.6 kPa, the
total pressure being 101.325 kPa. Moist air may be treated as an ideal gas mixture of water vapour
and dry air. The relation between saturation temperature ([latex]T_{s}[/latex]  in K) and saturation pressure ([latex]p_{s}[/latex]  in KPa) for water is given by [latex]ln(p_{s}/p_{o})[/latex]=14.317-5304/[latex]T_{s}[/latex] , where [latex]p_{o}[/latex] = 101.325 kPa. The dry
bulb temperature of the moist air sample (in [latex]^{\circ}[/latex] C) is __________
questions.explanation: Given data: Relative humidity, [latex] \phi=70 \%=0.70[/latex] Partial pressure, [latex] p_{v}=1.6 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex] Total pressure, [latex] p_{0}=101.325 \mathrm{kPa}[/latex] We know that, [latex] \begin{aligned} \phi&=\frac{p_{v}}{p_{s}}\\ 0.70 &=\frac{1.6}{p_{s}} \\ \text{or}\quad p_{s} &=\frac{1.6}{0.70}=2.2857 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}[/latex] Temperature corresponding to saturation pressure is dry bulb temperature, [latex] \begin{aligned} \ln \left\{\frac{p_{s}}{p_{o}}\right\} &=14.317-\frac{5304}{T_{s}} \\ \ln \left\{\frac{2.2857}{101.325}\right\} &=14.317-\frac{5304}{T_{s}} \\ -3.79166 &=14.317-\frac{5304}{T_{s}} \\ \frac{5304}{T_{s}} &=14.317+3.79166 \\ \frac{5304}{T_{s}} &=18.10866 \\ \text{or}\quad T_{s} &= 292.89 \mathrm{K}\\ &=(292.89-273)^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ &=19.89^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Gray cast iron blocks of size 100 mm x 50 mm x 10 mm with a central spherical cavity of diameter 4 mm are sand cast. The shrinkage allowance for the pattern is 3%. The ratio of the volume of the pattern to volume of the casting is _________
questions.explanation: Ratio of volume of pattern to volume of casting is given by [latex]=\frac{(1.03\times100)\times(1.03\times50)\times(1.03\times10)}{100\times50\times10}=1.093[/latex] Volume of cavity is assumed to be small and negligible as it will complicate the question to a higher level. If your answer was less than 1, read below. There are three things to be understood here :- 1. Liquid Shrinkage It refers to the reduction in volume when the metal changes from liquid state to solid state at the solidus temperature. The liquid shrinkage is rarely a problem, because the molten metal is continuously flowing in mold cavity and also riser to compensate the shrinkage of liquid in the cavity. 2. Solidification i.e Liquid to solid phase transformation (GCI expands in this process unlike other metals) So now during phase transformation gray cast iron expands (unlike other metals which contract) and there is no need of riser (used to take care of phase transformation shrinkage + liquid shrinkage). 3. Solid state Cooling (GCI contracts in this process just like other metals) It refers to the reduction in volume caused when metal loses temperature in solid state. To account for this, shrinkage allowance is provided on the patterns. The Shrinkage allowance depends primarily upon Coefficient of thermal expansion. For Grey CI in particular it is positive, it means solid grey cast iron expands on increasing temp and contracts on decreasing temperature just like any other metal. Adding all above factors Neglecting the Liquid shrinkage we see that GCI expands in during solidification and contracts when cooled in solid form. So the net result would be sum of them. According to NPTL in the table for GCI they have given the net value of shrinkage’s which is positive and hence the pattern size would be more than the casting. Note: The expansion of GCI during phase change (solidification) is a fact but at the same time we need to consider the contraction of GCI when cooling in solid state. So net result according to IISC and NPTEL is contraction so the size of pattern will be more than that of casting.
questions.explanation_html:
Ratio of volume of pattern to volume of casting is given by

[latex]=\frac{(1.03\times100)\times(1.03\times50)\times(1.03\times10)}{100\times50\times10}=1.093[/latex]

Volume of cavity is assumed to be small and negligible as it will complicate the question to a higher level.
If your answer was less than 1, read below.

There are three things to be understood here :-

1. Liquid Shrinkage
It refers to the reduction in volume when the metal changes from liquid state to solid state at the solidus temperature. The liquid shrinkage is rarely a problem, because the molten metal is continuously flowing in mold cavity and also riser to compensate the shrinkage of liquid in the cavity.

2. Solidification i.e Liquid to solid phase transformation (GCI expands in this process unlike other metals)
So now during phase transformation gray cast iron expands (unlike other metals which contract) and there is no need of riser (used to take care of phase transformation shrinkage + liquid shrinkage).

3. Solid state Cooling (GCI contracts in this process just like other metals)
It refers to the reduction in volume caused when metal loses temperature in solid state. To account for this, shrinkage allowance is provided on the patterns. The Shrinkage allowance depends primarily upon Coefficient of thermal expansion. For Grey CI in particular it is positive, it means solid grey cast iron expands on increasing temp and contracts on decreasing temperature just like any other metal.

Adding all above factors

Neglecting the Liquid shrinkage we see that GCI expands in during solidification and contracts when cooled in solid form. So the net result would be sum of them. According to NPTL in the table for GCI they have given the net value of shrinkage’s which is positive and hence the pattern size would be more than the casting.

Note: The expansion of GCI during phase change (solidification) is a fact but at the same time we need to consider the contraction of GCI when cooling in solid state. So net result according to IISC and NPTEL is contraction so the size of pattern will be more than that of casting.

At steady state
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q_{A} &=Q_{B} \\ \frac{k_{A}\left[T_{1}-T_{2}\right] A}{L_{1}} &=\frac{k_{B}\left[T_{2}-T_{3}\right] A}{L_{2}} \\ \frac{20 \times\left[130-T_{2}\right]}{0.1} &=\frac{100 \times\left[T_{2}-30\right]}{0.3} \\ 3\left[130-T_{2}\right] &=5 T_{2}-150 \\ 390-3 T_{2} &=5 T_{2}-150 \\ 540 &=8 T_{2} \\ T_{2} &=67.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.explanation: In a wire-cut EDM process, a thin metallic wire is fed on to the conducting workpiece, which is submerged in a tank of dielectric fluid such as de-ionized water. Wire is fed in the programmed path & material is cut from the workpiece accordingly. Material removal takes place by a series of discrete discharges between the wire electrode & workpiece in the presence of a dielectric fluid. The di-electric fluid gets ionized in between the tool electrode gap thereby creating a  path for each discharge. The area wherein discharge takes place gets heated to very high temperature such that the surface get melted & removed. The cut particles (debris) get flushed away by continuous flowing dielectric fluid. Generally, wire-cut EDM is used for cutting Aluminium, brass, etc. & wire material used for quicker cutting action is zinc coated brass wires.

questions.question: The value of the line integral [latex]\oint_{c}\bar{F}\cdot \bar{r'} \; ds[/latex] ,where C is a circle of radius [latex]4/\sqrt{\pi}[/latex] unit is ___ Here, [latex]\bar{F}(x,y)= y\hat{i}+2x\hat{j} \; and \; \bar{r}'[/latex] is the UNIT tangent vector on the curve C at an arc length s from a reference point on the curve. [latex]\hat{i}[/latex]  and [latex]\hat{j}[/latex] are the basis vectors in the x-y Cartesian reference. In evaluating the line integral, the curve has to be traversed in the counter-clockwise direction.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \int_{c} \bar{F} \cdot \vec{r}\acute{} d x=\int_{c} \bar{F} \cdot & d \bar{r}=\int_{c} F_{1} d x+F_{2} d y \\ &=\iint_{R}\left(\frac{\partial F_{2}}{d x}-\frac{\partial F_{1}}{d y}\right) d x d y \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{rl} F_{1}=y & F_{2}=2 x \\ & =\iint_{R}(2-1) d x d y \end{array} \\ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial y}=1 \quad \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x} &=2 \\ &=\iint d x d y \end{aligned} \end{array}\\ &=\text { Area of the circle with radius } \frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}=\pi\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^{2}\\ &=\pi \frac{16}{\pi}=16 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: An inextensible massless string goes over a frictionless pulley. Two weights of 100 N and 200 N are attached to the two ends of the string. The weights are released from rest, and start moving due to gravity. The tension in the string (in N) is __________

questions.question: A single degree of freedom spring-mass system is subjected to a harmonic force of constant amplitude. For an excitation frequency of [latex]\sqrt{3k/m}[/latex] the ratio of the amplitude of steady state response to the static deflection of the spring is __________
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{A}{x_{0}} &=\text { Magnification factor } \\ \frac{A}{F_{0} / k} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{\omega}{w_{n}}\right)^{2}+\left(2 \zeta \frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}\right)^{2}}} \\ \because \qquad \zeta &=0 \\ \frac{A}{F_{0} / k} &=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}\right)^{2}-1} \\ \omega &=\sqrt{\frac{3 k}{m}}, \quad \omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \\ \frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}} &=\sqrt{\frac{3 k}{m}} \times \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} \\ &=\sqrt{3} \\ \frac{A}{F_{0} / k} &=\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}-1}=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{A}{x_{0}} &=\text { Magnification factor } \\ \frac{A}{F_{0} / k} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{\omega}{w_{n}}\right)^{2}+\left(2 \zeta \frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}\right)^{2}}} \\ \because \qquad \zeta &=0 \\ \frac{A}{F_{0} / k} &=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}}\right)^{2}-1} \\ \omega &=\sqrt{\frac{3 k}{m}}, \quad \omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \\ \frac{\omega}{\omega_{n}} &=\sqrt{\frac{3 k}{m}} \times \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} \\ &=\sqrt{3} \\ \frac{A}{F_{0} / k} &=\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}-1}=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider a fully developed steady laminar flow of an incompressible fluid with viscosity [latex]\mu[/latex] through a circular pipe of radius R. Given that the velocity at a radial location of R/2 from the centerline of the pipe is [latex]U_{1}[/latex], the shear stress at the wall is [latex]K\mu U_{1}/R[/latex], where K is __________
questions.explanation: Shear stress at the wall, [latex] \tau_{0}=\tau_{\max }=\frac{k \mu U_{1}}{R}[/latex] We know that the velocity at any point for laminar flow through pipe, [latex] \begin{aligned} u&=-\frac{1}{4 \mu}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right)\left(R^{2}-r^{2}\right)\\ \mathrm{At} \quad r&=\frac{R}{2}, u=U_{1}\\ \therefore \quad U_{1} &=-\frac{1}{4 \mu}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right)\left(R^{2}-\frac{R^{2}}{4}\right) \\ &=-\frac{1}{4 \mu}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) \frac{3}{4} R^{2} \\ &=-\frac{3}{16 \mu}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) R^{2}\\ \therefore \tau_{0}&=-\frac{K \mu}{R} \times \frac{3}{16 \mu}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) R^{2}\\ \tau_{0}&=-\frac{3}{16} K\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) R\\ \end{aligned}[/latex] We know that maximum shear stress at wall. [latex] \tau_{0}=-\frac{R \partial p}{\partial} \frac{\partial p}{\partial x}[/latex] [latex] \therefore-\frac{3}{16} K\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) R=-\frac{R}{2} \frac{\partial p}{\partial x} [/latex] [latex] \text{or}K=\frac{8}{3}=2.66[/latex]

Shear stress at the wall,

questions.question: Two large parallel plates having a gap of 10 mm in between them are maintained at temperatures  T1 = 1000 K and T2 = 400 K. Given emissivity values, [latex]\varepsilon{1}=0.5[/latex] ,  [latex]\varepsilon_{2}=0.25[/latex]  and Stefan-Boltzmann constant [latex]\sigma= 5.67 \times 10^{-8} W/m^{2}-K^{4}[/latex], the heat transfer between the plates (in kW/[latex]m^{2}[/latex]) is __________ _________
questions.explanation: [latex] \begin{aligned} Q &=\frac{\sigma\left[T_{1}^{4}-T_{2}^{4}\right]}{\frac{1}{\epsilon_{1}}+\frac{1}{\epsilon_{2}}-1}=\frac{5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times\left(1000^{4}-400^{4}\right)}{\frac{1}{0.5}+\frac{1}{0.25}-1} \\ &=11049.7 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2}=11.05 \mathrm{kW} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html: [latex] \begin{aligned} Q &=\frac{\sigma\left[T_{1}^{4}-T_{2}^{4}\right]}{\frac{1}{\epsilon_{1}}+\frac{1}{\epsilon_{2}}-1}=\frac{5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times\left(1000^{4}-400^{4}\right)}{\frac{1}{0.5}+\frac{1}{0.25}-1} \\ &=11049.7 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2}=11.05 \mathrm{kW} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: A cylindrical steel rod, 0.01 m in diameter and 0.2 m in length is first heated to [latex]750^{\circ}C[/latex]  and then immersed in a water bath at [latex]100^{\circ}C[/latex] .  The heat transfer coefficient is 250 W/[latex]m^{2}[/latex]-K. The density, specific heat and thermal conductivity of steel are [latex]\rho = 7801 kg/m^{3}[/latex], c = 473 J/kg-K, and  k = 43 W/m-K, respectively.  The time required for the rod to reach [latex]300^{\circ}C[/latex]  is ________  seconds.
questions.explanation: Given data: [latex] \mathrm{D}=0.01 \mathrm{m} ; \quad L=0.2 \mathrm{m} ; \quad T_{i}=750^{\circ} \mathrm{C} [/latex] [latex] T_{\infty}=100^{\circ} \mathrm{C} ; \quad h=250 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} ; \quad \rho=7801 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex] [latex] \mathrm{c}=473 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kgK} [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{T-T_{\infty}}{T_{i}-T_{\infty}}&=\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{h A t}{\rho V c}}\\\text{ Where }\quad \frac{V}{A}&=\frac{\pi D^{2} L}{4 \times \pi D L}=\frac{D}{4}=\frac{0.01}{4} \\ &=2.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \frac{300-100}{750-100}&=e^{\frac{-250 \times t}{7801 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 473}} \\ \frac{200}{650}&=e^{-0.0271 t} \\ 0.30769&=e^{-0.0271 t}\end{aligned}[/latex] Taking [latex]  \log _{e} [/latex] both sides, we get [latex]\begin{aligned}  \log _{e} 0.30769&=-0.0271 t \log _{e} e \\ &\qquad\left(\because \log _{\theta} e=1\right) \\ t&=\frac{1.1786}{0.027}=43.65 \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Given data:
[latex] \mathrm{D}=0.01 \mathrm{m} ; \quad L=0.2 \mathrm{m} ; \quad T_{i}=750^{\circ} \mathrm{C} [/latex]
[latex] T_{\infty}=100^{\circ} \mathrm{C} ; \quad h=250 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} ; \quad \rho=7801 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3} [/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{c}=473 \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kgK} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{T-T_{\infty}}{T_{i}-T_{\infty}}&=\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{h A t}{\rho V c}}\\\text{ Where }\quad \frac{V}{A}&=\frac{\pi D^{2} L}{4 \times \pi D L}=\frac{D}{4}=\frac{0.01}{4} \\ &=2.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{m} \\ \therefore \frac{300-100}{750-100}&=e^{\frac{-250 \times t}{7801 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 473}} \\ \frac{200}{650}&=e^{-0.0271 t} \\ 0.30769&=e^{-0.0271 t}\end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking [latex] \log _{e} [/latex] both sides, we get
[latex]\begin{aligned} \log _{e} 0.30769&=-0.0271 t \log _{e} e \\ &\qquad\left(\because \log _{\theta} e=1\right) \\ t&=\frac{1.1786}{0.027}=43.65 \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] h_{1}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2}+g z_{1}+q=h_{2}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2}+g_{2}+w [/latex] where q=0 insulated nozzle [latex] z_{1}=z_{2} \quad[/latex] horizontal nozzle w=0  always for nozzle [latex] \begin{aligned} h_{1}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2} &=h_{2}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2} \\ h_{1}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2000} &=h_{2}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2000} \end{aligned}[/latex] where [latex] h_{1}[/latex] and [latex]h_{2}[/latex] are in kJ/kg and [latex]V_{1}[/latex] and [latex]V_{2}[/latex] are in m/s [latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore 100+\frac{(100)^{2}}{2000} &=h_{2}+\frac{(200)^{2}}{2000} \\ 100+5 &=h_{2}+20 \\ \text{or}\quad h_{2} &=85 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: In a 3-stage air compressor, the inlet pressure is [latex]p_{1}[/latex], discharge pressure is [latex]p_{4}[/latex] and the intermediate pressures are [latex]p_{2}[/latex] and [latex]p_{3}[/latex] ( [latex]p_{2}\lt p_{3}[/latex]). [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{p_{4}}{p_{3}} \times \frac{p_{3}}{p_{2}} \times \frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}&=10 \\ r_{p} \times r_{p} \times r_{p}&=10 \\ r_{p}^{3} &=10 \\ r_{p} &=(10)^{1 / 3}\\ p_{2}&=r_{p} p_{1} \\ p_{3}&=r_{p} p_{2}=r_{p}^{2} p_{1}=(10)^{2 / 3} \times 100\\ &=464.16 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{p_{4}}{p_{1}}&=10 \\ \frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}&=\frac{p_{3}}{p_{2}}=\frac{p_{4}}{p_{3}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
To calculate [latex]p_{3}=? [/latex]

questions.question: In the vapour compression cycle shown in the figure, the evaporating and condensing temperatures are 260 K and 310 K, respectively. The compressor takes in liquid-vapour mixture (state 1) and isentropically compresses it to a dry saturated vapour condition (state 2). The specific heat of the liquid refrigerant is 4.8 kJ/kg-K and may be treated as constant. The enthalpy of evaporation for the refrigerant at 310 K is 1054 kJ/kg. The difference between the enthalpies at state points 1 and 0 (in kJ/kg) is ____________
questions.explanation: Given data: [latex] \begin{aligned} T_{e} &=260 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{c} &=310 \mathrm{K} \\ c_{p l} &=4.8 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ h_{fg} &=1054 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \text { at } T_{c}=310 \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex] Taking reference temperature T , at which entropy is [latex] s_{T} [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad s_{3}-s_{T} &=c \ln \frac{T_{3}}{T} \\ s_{3} &=s_{T}+c \ln \frac{T_{3}}{T}=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T} \\ \text { Similarly, } s_{0} &=s_{T}+c \ln \frac{260}{T}=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{260}{T} \\ \therefore \quad s_{2}-s_{3} &=\frac{h_{f g}}{T}=\frac{1054}{310} \\ s_{2} &=s_{3}+\frac{1054}{310} \end{aligned}[/latex] Substitute the value of [latex]s_{3}[/latex] in above equation, we get [latex] \begin{aligned} s_{2} &=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T}+\frac{1054}{310} \\ s_{2} &=s_{1} \\ s_{1} &=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T}+\frac{1054}{310} \\ h_{1}-h_{0} &=T_{e}\left[s_{1}-s_{0}\right] \\ =& 260 \times\left[s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T}+\frac{1054}{310}\right.\\ &\left.-s_{T}-4.8 \ln \frac{260}{T}\right] \\ &=260\left[4.8 \ln \left(\frac{310}{T} \times \frac{T}{260}\right)+\frac{1054}{310}\right] \\ &1103.51\mathrm{kJ}/\mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given data:
[latex] \begin{aligned} T_{e} &=260 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{c} &=310 \mathrm{K} \\ c_{p l} &=4.8 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ h_{fg} &=1054 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \text { at } T_{c}=310 \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Taking reference temperature T , at which entropy is [latex] s_{T} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad s_{3}-s_{T} &=c \ln \frac{T_{3}}{T} \\ s_{3} &=s_{T}+c \ln \frac{T_{3}}{T}=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T} \\ \text { Similarly, } s_{0} &=s_{T}+c \ln \frac{260}{T}=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{260}{T} \\ \therefore \quad s_{2}-s_{3} &=\frac{h_{f g}}{T}=\frac{1054}{310} \\ s_{2} &=s_{3}+\frac{1054}{310} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substitute the value of [latex]s_{3}[/latex] in above equation, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} s_{2} &=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T}+\frac{1054}{310} \\ s_{2} &=s_{1} \\ s_{1} &=s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T}+\frac{1054}{310} \\ h_{1}-h_{0} &=T_{e}\left[s_{1}-s_{0}\right] \\ =& 260 \times\left[s_{T}+4.8 \ln \frac{310}{T}+\frac{1054}{310}\right.\\ &\left.-s_{T}-4.8 \ln \frac{260}{T}\right] \\ &=260\left[4.8 \ln \left(\frac{310}{T} \times \frac{T}{260}\right)+\frac{1054}{310}\right] \\ &1103.51\mathrm{kJ}/\mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: A point P(1,3,-5) is translated by [latex]2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-4\hat{k}[/latex] and then rotated counter clockwise by [latex]90^{\circ}[/latex]  about the z-axis. The new position of the point is
questions.explanation: Initial point is (1, 3, -5) After tranlated by 2i+3j-4k, it becomes =(1+2, 3+3, -5-4)= (3, 6, -9) Rotation by 90 CCW about z axis (NOTE: : when rotated about z-axis the z component will remain same.) Hence the point (3, 6, -9) changes to (-6, 3, -9).

A firm uses a turning center, a milling center and a grinding machine to produce two parts. The table below provides the machining time required for each part and the maximum machining time available on each machine. The profit per unit on parts I and II are Rs. 40 and Rs. 100, respectively. The maximum profit per week of the firm is Rs._________
questions.explanation: The question will be solved using the graphical method [latex]\text{Maximize } Z=40X_1+100X_2[/latex] Constraints are [latex]\begin{aligned} 12X_1+6X_2 \leq 6000 \\ 4X_1+10X_2 \leq 4000 \\ 2X_1+3X_2 \leq 1800 \\ X_1,X_2 \geq 0 \end{aligned}[/latex] We have three corner points as follow [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{At }(0,400)\;\;\;&Z=40,000\\ \text{At }(375,250)\;\;\;&Z=40,000\\ \text{At }(500,100)\;\;\;&Z=20,000 \end{aligned}[/latex] Hence, maximum profit per week is 40,000.
questions.explanation_html:
The question will be solved using the graphical method

[latex]\text{Maximize } Z=40X_1+100X_2[/latex]

Constraints are
[latex]\begin{aligned} 12X_1+6X_2 \leq 6000 \\ 4X_1+10X_2 \leq 4000 \\ 2X_1+3X_2 \leq 1800 \\ X_1,X_2 \geq 0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
We have three corner points as follow
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{At }(0,400)\;\;\;&Z=40,000\\ \text{At }(375,250)\;\;\;&Z=40,000\\ \text{At }(500,100)\;\;\;&Z=20,000 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Hence, maximum profit per week is 40,000.
